answers.answer: Test $H_0:\mu_D-\mu_E=0$ versus $H_a:\mu_D-\mu_E\ne0$. Welch's standard error is $\sqrt{18^2/8+20^2/10}=8.972$, so $t=(41-45)/8.972=-0.446$ with approximately 15.7 degrees of freedom. The two-sided p-value is about 0.662. Fail to reject $H_0$; there is no evidence that the mean lifetimes differ.

Test $H_0:\mu_G-\mu_P=0$ versus $H_a:\mu_G-\mu_P>0$. Welch's standard error is $\sqrt{0.6^2/104+0.5^2/115}=0.0751$, so $t=(5.7-5.5)/0.0751=2.664$ with approximately 201 degrees of freedom. The one-sided p-value is about 0.0042. Reject $H_0$; the data support an increase in mean memory score.

The pooled variance is $s_p^2=[5(3.3^2)+5(2.1^2)]/10=7.65$. Thus $\operatorname{SE}=\sqrt{7.65(1/6+1/6)}=1.5969$ and $t=(77.4-72.2)/1.5969=3.256$ with $df=10$. The one-sided p-value is about 0.0043, so reject $H_0$; there is evidence that $\mu_1>\mu_2$.

The sample means are 17.4 and 15.1, with sample variances 3.6 and 10.1. The pooled variance is 6.85, so $\operatorname{SE}=1.1705$ and $t=(17.4-15.1)/1.1705=1.965$ with $df=18$. The two-sided p-value is about 0.0650. Fail to reject equality at 0.05.

Test $H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2\le0$ versus $H_a:\mu_1-\mu_2>0$. The pooled variance is 1422.32, giving $\operatorname{SE}=13.802$ and $t=25/13.802=1.811$ with $df=28$. The p-value is about 0.0404, so reject $H_0$; the data support the manufacturer's claim.

Test $H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2\le0$ versus $H_a:\mu_1-\mu_2>0$. Welch's standard error is $2.4309$, $t=5.1/2.4309=2.098$, and $df\approx30.84$. The one-sided p-value is about 0.0221. Reject $H_0$ at 0.10; the data support the personnel director's claim.

Define improvement differences $d=\text{Without}-\text{With}$: $1.9,2.1,1.7,0.3,1.1,2.9,1.8,1.9,0.8$. Then $\bar d=1.6111$, $s_d=0.7705$, and $t=6.273$ with $df=8$ for $H_0:\mu_d=0$ versus $H_a:\mu_d>0$. The p-value is about 0.00012, so reject $H_0$; the additive improves mileage. A 90% CI for mean improvement is approximately $[1.134,2.089]$ mpg.

Let $d=B-A=(-5,24,-6,9,10,14,-1,-7)$. Then $\bar d=4.75$, $s_d=11.235$, and $t=1.196$ with $df=7$ for $H_0:\mu_d=0$ versus $H_a:\mu_d>0$. The one-sided p-value is 0.135, so fail to reject $H_0$. The 95% CI is $4.75\pm2.365(11.235/\sqrt8)=[-4.642,14.142]$ minutes.

Let $d=\text{After}-\text{Before}=(36,8,32,4,9,29,-13,0,-2,9)$. Then $\bar d=11.2$, $s_d=16.061$, and $t=2.205$ with $df=9$ for a two-sided test. The p-value is about 0.0549, so fail to reject $H_0:\mu_d=0$ at 0.05; evidence of a mean difference is just insufficient.

Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be the two-year and seven-month proportions. Test $H_0:p_1=p_2$ versus $H_a:p_1\ne p_2$. The sample proportions are 0.0649 and 0.2262; pooled $\hat p=24/161=0.1491$, giving $z=-2.870$ and two-sided p-value 0.0041. Reject $H_0$; the proportions differ, with more episodes in the seven-month group.

Test $H_0:p_{CA}=p_{OR}$ versus $H_a:p_{CA}<p_{OR}$. The pooled standard error gives $z=-1.427$ and one-sided p-value 0.0768. Fail to reject $H_0$ at 0.05; evidence is insufficient that California's smoking proportion is lower.

a. For finance, $\hat p=81/178=0.4551$. Test $H_0:p\ge0.50$ versus $H_a:p<0.50$. Using $p_0=0.5$, $z=-1.199$ and p-value 0.115. Fail to reject; the sample does not show that fewer than half hold the view.

b. The accounting proportion is $75/148=0.5068$. A pooled two-proportion test gives $z=0.930$ and two-sided p-value 0.352. Fail to reject equality; there is no significant difference.
